dryRun.title: /(?<user>[\w.]+)@(?<domain>\w+\.com)/ on "mail a.b@site.com now"
dryRun.note: A regex describes a text pattern. Key pieces: character classes (\d \w \s [a-z]), quantifiers (* + ? {2,4}, add ? to make them lazy), anchors (^ $ \b), groups (( ), named (?<n>)), lookarounds ((?=…)). Flags: g (all), i (ignore case), m (multiline), u (unicode).

why: With g, match returns every match. Without g it returns the first match with its details (index, groups).
.* is greedy and runs to the last . .*? is lazy and stops at the first.
A global regex remembers lastIndex between test() calls: 0 → 1 → 2 (no match, resets to 0). Do not reuse /g regexes for test().
$1… refer to groups in the replacement. (?=$) is a lookahead: digits right before the end. A function replacement computes the new text.

think.q: You build a regex from user input "a.b" to find that exact text. What must you do?
opts: Escape special characters first, or "." matches any character
why: Escape with s.replace(/[.*+?^${}()|[\]\\]/g, "\\$&") before new RegExp(s).

try.task: Write parseLogLine(line) for lines like "2026-10-24 12:30:05 [ERROR] db: timeout after 30s": return { date, time, level, source, message }, or null if the line does not match. Use one regex with named groups.
try.hint: Anchor with ^ and $; levels are capital letters; source is \w+; message is the rest (.+).

checks.verify: const r = parseLogLine("2026-10-24 12:30:05 [ERROR] db: timeout after 30s"); assert(r && r.date === "2026-10-24" && r.time === "12:30:05" && r.level === "ERROR" && r.source === "db" && r.message === "timeout after 30s", JSON.stringify(r))
assert(parseLogLine("garbage") === null && parseLogLine("2026-10-24 12:30:05 ERROR db: x") === null, "null")

checks.t: message may contain colons and brackets
checks.verify: const r = parseLogLine("2026-01-01 00:00:00 [INFO] api: GET /x [200]: ok"); assert(r && r.message === "GET /x [200]: ok", "message")

takeaway.key: Classes, quantifiers (greedy vs lazy), anchors, groups, lookarounds and flags. Escape user input, and beware lastIndex on /g regexes.
mistakes: Building a regex from unescaped user input.

dryRun.title: One instant, many views: new Date(Date.UTC(2026, 0, 31, 20, 0))
dryRun.note: A Date is one instant in time (a UTC timestamp). Time zones only matter when you display or parse. Store and send ISO strings in UTC; format with Intl.DateTimeFormat and an explicit timeZone. Temporal is the modern API that fixes most Date problems.

think.q:
const d = new Date(Date.UTC(2026, 0, 31, 20, 0))
const f = (tz) => new Intl.DateTimeFormat('en-GB', { timeZone: tz, dateStyle: 'medium', timeStyle: 'short' }).format(d)
console.log(f('Asia/Kolkata') + ' | ' + f('America/New_York'))
why: Same instant, different wall clocks. India is UTC+5:30, so it is already 1 February there.
31 February does not exist, so it rolls over into March. Adding months needs care (clamp to the last day).
Months are 0-based (11 = December). An invalid date has time NaN, it does not throw.

think.q:
const a = new Date('2026-03-01T00:00:00Z'), b = new Date('2026-03-08T00:00:00Z')
console.log((b - a) / 86400000, a < b)
why: Subtracting Dates gives milliseconds. Comparisons work because Dates convert to numbers.

think.q: new Date("2026-03-01") vs new Date("2026-03-01T00:00"): what is the trap?
opts: The date-only form is parsed as UTC, the date-time form as local time
why: Always include an explicit zone (Z or +05:30) in strings you parse.

try.task: Write addMonthsClamped(isoDate, n) for date-only strings (UTC): add n months and clamp to the last day of the target month. Also write daysBetween(a, b) for two ISO dates.
try.hint: Get y, m, d in UTC; the last day of a month is new Date(Date.UTC(y, m + 1, 0)).getUTCDate().

checks.t: clamps to the end of a short month

takeaway.key: A Date is a UTC instant. Store/send ISO UTC strings, format with Intl and an explicit timeZone, remember months start at 0, and handle month-end rollovers.
mistakes: Adding months with setMonth and landing in the next month.
Using local getters (getHours) when you meant UTC.
